title: 1 Samuel 9:1–14
context: The narrative turns to Saul, the impressive and tall son of Kish, a Benjamite man of valor. Sent by his father to look for lost donkeys, Saul and a servant wander through several districts without success. When Saul wants to turn back, the servant suggests consulting a man of God in a nearby city, and they bring a small gift of silver. Young women drawing water direct them to the seer, who has come to bless a sacrifice at the high place, and Samuel comes out toward them as they enter the city. Both traditions read this ordinary errand as the setting in which God’s purpose quietly unfolds through human choices and seemingly chance events.

verses.text: Now there was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Becorath, the son of Aphiah, the son of a Benjamite, a mighty man of valor.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Saul is introduced through his father Kish, a Benjamite of standing and strength. The narrative grounds the coming king in a real family and tribe, and the story that follows will show how much depends on how this promising man responds to the calling he receives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the genealogy places Saul in Benjamin rather than in Judah, the tribe linked with royal promise (Genesis 49:10). Without diminishing Saul, the detail hints that this first king answers the people’s request, while God’s longer purpose for kingship will run through another line.

verses.text: He had a son whose name was Saul, an impressive young man; and there was not among the children of Israel a more handsome person than he. From his shoulders and upward he was taller than any of the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Saul’s impressive appearance and height as real gifts that fit him for public leadership. Yet outward qualities do not guarantee faithfulness, and the story will show that what Saul does with his gifts matters as much as the gifts themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul is exactly the kind of king the people might choose by sight: handsome and taller than anyone. Later the LORD will say that he looks on the heart rather than outward appearance (1 Samuel 16:7), a contrast both traditions see the narrator preparing here.

verses.text: The donkeys of Kish, Saul’s father, were lost. Kish said to Saul his son, “Now take one of the servants with you, and arise, go look for the donkeys.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the ordinariness of the errand: lost donkeys and a father’s simple instruction. God’s call often meets people in the middle of everyday duties, and Saul’s obedience to his father is a small but genuine act within which a larger calling will soon be offered.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the lost donkeys a classic example of providence working through ordinary events. Nothing in the errand looks significant, yet God is guiding the circumstances to bring Saul to Samuel, as the LORD will reveal to Samuel in 9:15–16.

verses.text: He passed through the hill country of Ephraim, and passed through the land of Shalishah, but they didn’t find them. Then they passed through the land of Shaalim, and they weren’t there. Then he passed through the land of the Benjamites, but they didn’t find them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe the extended and frustrating search through Ephraim, Shalishah, Shaalim, and Benjamin. The failure of human effort is not presented as meaningless; it is the path by which Saul comes to the place where God will meet him, and Saul keeps going rather than giving up at once.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the repeated “they didn’t find them” moves Saul step by step toward Samuel’s city. The exact locations of Shalishah and Shaalim are uncertain, but the point is clear: apparent failure is woven into God’s guidance of events.

verses.text: When they had come to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant who was with him, “Come! Let’s return, lest my father stop caring about the donkeys and be anxious for us.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Saul’s considerate concern that his father will start worrying about him rather than the donkeys. He is portrayed sympathetically at the outset, a young man with real virtues whose later choices will be all the more tragic for that.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Saul is ready to give up just as he reaches the land of Zuph, a region whose exact location is uncertain but which may connect with Samuel’s family background (1 Samuel 1:1). Human plans to turn back are overruled by the guidance that brings Saul to the seer.

verses.text: The servant said to him, “Behold now, there is a man of God in this city, and he is a man who is held in honor. All that he says surely happens. Now let’s go there. Perhaps he can tell us which way to go.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers highlight the servant’s initiative: he knows of an honored man of God whose word surely comes to pass. God’s purposes often advance through the counsel of ordinary people, and Saul’s willingness to listen to his servant is a genuine and fruitful choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the servant, not Saul, knows of the man of God and suggests going to him. God uses an unnamed servant to steer events, and the description of the prophet whose words surely happen affirms the reliability of God’s word through his messenger.

verses.text: Then Saul said to his servant, “But behold, if we go, what should we bring the man? For the bread is spent in our sacks, and there is not a present to bring to the man of God. What do we have?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Saul’s concern about bringing a present as a sign of respect and social custom. He does not presume on the man of God, and his hesitation shows a man aware of his own lack, which the narrative presents with gentle realism.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note Saul’s practical concern that they have nothing to bring. The future king does not yet seem to know Samuel or to seek God directly; he is pursuing donkeys, while God is pursuing a purpose he has not yet disclosed to Saul.

verses.text: The servant answered Saul again and said, “Behold, I have in my hand the fourth part of a shekel of silver. I will give that to the man of God, to tell us our way.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the servant’s readiness to give his own small piece of silver, the fourth part of a shekel. Generosity and initiative from an unexpected person open the way forward, and the scene shows God working through freely offered gifts and choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that a small coin in a servant’s hand becomes the means of bringing Saul to his anointing. Both traditions find the detail vivid: God’s great purposes often turn on humble and seemingly incidental human actions.

verses.text: (In earlier times in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he said, “Come! Let’s go to the seer;” for he who is now called a prophet was before called a seer.)
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the narrator’s aside explaining that a prophet was formerly called a seer. The parenthesis shows the account was written or edited for later readers, helping them understand older terms, and it underlines that the person Saul seeks speaks with God’s authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the aside about seer and prophet as a note for later readers. It emphasizes that inquiring of God through his appointed messenger was a recognized practice, and it frames Samuel as the one through whom God will make his will known in this story.

verses.text: Then Saul said to his servant, “Well said. Come! Let’s go.” So they went to the city where the man of God was.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Saul’s quick agreement: “Well said. Come! Let’s go.” A willingness to act on good counsel is a real virtue, and the narrative shows Saul freely choosing to go to the man of God at this point in his story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Saul’s agreement moves the account toward its divinely appointed meeting. Saul freely chooses to go, and that free choice is the very means God uses to accomplish what he has already revealed to Samuel, a pairing both traditions affirm in their own terms.

verses.text: As they went up the ascent to the city, they found young maidens going out to draw water, and said to them, “Is the seer here?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the young women drawing water who answer the travelers’ question. Ordinary people going about daily tasks are part of how Saul finds his way, and their ready help adds to the sense of a community through which God works.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the meeting with women at the water may recall other water-drawing scenes in Genesis and Exodus, though here it leads to a prophet rather than a bride. The detail adds to the sense that every step of Saul’s journey is being guided toward Samuel.

verses.text: They answered them and said, “He is. Behold, he is before you. Hurry now, for he has come today into the city; for the people have a sacrifice today in the high place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe the timing: Samuel has come into the city that very day for a sacrifice at the high place. The young women urge haste, and Saul’s readiness to respond to their urging is part of how he arrives at the right moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the timing as a further sign of providence: Samuel arrives today for the sacrifice, just as Saul arrives. The high place here appears to be a legitimate local site of worship in this period, before worship was centralized in Jerusalem, a point readers in both traditions often note.

verses.text: As soon as you have come into the city, you will immediately find him before he goes up to the high place to eat; for the people will not eat until he comes, because he blesses the sacrifice. Afterwards those who are invited eat. Now therefore go up; for at this time you will find him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the people wait to eat until the seer blesses the sacrifice. Samuel holds a respected spiritual role in the community, and Saul is about to enter that setting of worship and fellowship where God’s purpose will be made known to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the sacrifice and shared meal place Saul’s calling within worship. The seer blesses the sacrifice before the invited guests eat, and Saul is about to be welcomed as an honored guest at a table prepared with him in mind.

verses.text: They went up to the city. As they came within the city, behold, Samuel came out toward them to go up to the high place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that as Saul and his servant enter the city, Samuel comes out toward them. The meeting arises from a convergence of choices, Saul seeking donkeys and Samuel going to the high place, in which God is actively at work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the meeting as the moment God’s hidden guidance becomes visible: just as Saul enters, Samuel comes out toward him. The narrator will next explain that the LORD had already told Samuel this would happen, so the encounter is anything but accidental.
